title: Nico and the Cat of Chaos
markdown:
Nico the jackdaw adjusted his spectacles until they threw two small suns and entered The Campus Chronicle with a decree in his walk. Tonight would be sophisticated. No last-minute panic, no haphazard scribbles. The office would hum with intellectual pursuit: the tap of keys, the rumour of parchment, perhaps a civilised ghost of coffee. He had been appointed Chief Editor. He meant to fill the title as one fills a well-cut coat. In his satchel, in a velvet-lined box, lay emergency spare spectacles, in case ink or wind presumed.

“Good evening, Nico!”

The voice was bright and a fraction too loud. Ada the cat sat on a stack of old magazines, grooming a paw as if it were theatre. Midnight fur, a dusting that might have been stardust, emerald eyes keeping constellations as secrets. She had borrowed oversized party headphones and looked like a furry satellite dish. She hummed a jazz nursery rhyme, complete with scat.

“Ada.” Nico’s voice was a bow tie tied a notch too far. “Deadline nights are for focused work, not improvisational serenades.”

Ada blinked, slow mischief. “Just enjoying the creative vortex.” Her tail flicked a paperclip into exile. “I heard polish. Thought I’d lend sparkle.” The tail nearly felled a tower of unused art supplies dying of boredom.

Nico sighed a sigh that had done overtime. Sparkle was the enemy. He wanted gravitas. He had been studying French idioms so a well-placed je ne sais quoi might lift the sports page into erudition. He had a list of approved fonts, each chosen for understated brilliance.

He sat at the ancient typewriter, relic and altar. The keys still smelled faintly of oil and old ambition. Finish the linguistics piece on obscure proverbs. Proof the editorials until even the conjunctions behaved. Layout impeccable, columns as straight as a well-argued footnote. A crystal vase held one perfect rose, a quiet flag of beauty planted in chaos.

He might have asked Ada to leave. He did not. Crossing that small threshold—staying, with her in the room—felt like stepping off a map he had drawn in fountain pen.

Then the steam rose. Not Earl Grey. The communal coffee machine staged a rebellion against measured caffeine. A thick cloud haloed the serious faces of the few other students, a murky séance of deadlines.

Ada helped with layout by batting paperclips, pouncing on pens, and rearranging anything not nailed down. Nico watched his vision crumble faster than a croissant left in weather. He imagined his fonts weeping.

“Nico.” A weary voice from the back, sand in it. “There’s a rather significant typo in the lead of the science feature.”

His heart went down a well. He had proofed that section three times, magnifying glass, stern beak. Shoes clicked worry on linoleum. There it was, bold: not a comma’s indiscretion but a mangled word, amateur shouting from the rooftops.

“Oh, dear,” Nico murmured, heat crawling his neck, pale beak going pink.

“‘Oh, dear’ doesn’t cover it.” Ada nudged his elbow, appearing as she always did at the awkward minute. “Someone reached for quantum entanglement and landed on quaintly enthralled. A leap. Though I like the sound. Whimsical.”

Nico winced. “I asked for subtlety and received a banner. A loud one.” He had followed every rule.

The room held still except for the coffee machine’s mocking hiss. Nico wanted a corner and his feather collection, sorted by length until the world behaved. This was not polished. This was a mess. The ordeal was not the typo. It was the proof that control had missed what was in front of his perfectly polished lenses.

Ada hopped onto the desk, tail a small conductor’s baton, playfulness clocked off. “Show me the offending word. I have an eye for visual disruption. Sometimes the wrongness is how the letters sit.”

Before he could lecture on editorial sanctity she nudged the paragraph with her nose. “This letter is upside down. Tiny confused comma. This one has coffee on it. Startled badger. And the spacing is rude. They’re elbowing.”

Nico blinked. Semantics had blinded him. Ada, busker of chaos, was seeing. He had wanted faculty-impressing perfection. What he needed was a paper that could go out in the morning.

He took an eraser. Ada, dextrous when it mattered, lifted a fleck of escaped ink with a discarded receipt. Leo, a quiet graphic-design major who had been studying the ceiling, came alive and retyped the sentence as if he had been training for this exact disgrace. Chaos turned collaborative, a frantic useful dance. They were not defending the decorative article. They were fixing the one that had to exist by dawn. Nico even tilted the rose toward Leo, a camaraderie he would not have packed that morning.

The hidden cost arrived on the road back: his French idioms and font list had survived, immaculate and beside the point. The night’s real work had ink under the claws.

Hours later, pink and gold found the grimy windows. The corrected pages went. Nico sat, exhaustion a rumpled blanket. The office was still messy. The coffee machine gurgled a triumphant sigh. The air, though, had dropped its pretension. It felt shared. Real.

Ada curled on a discarded paper, a purr travelling the desk. “See? A little well-intentioned chaos shows you the way. Like a stray moonbeam finding the nap.”

Nico looked at the stack. The proverb article was there, punctuated to a fare-thee-well. It was the science feature—the near-disaster, the many-pawed salvage—that sat like an achievement. He had not got elegance. He had got a competent paper from an imperfect evening. In the same office where he had entered with twin suns on his spectacles, he left the spare pair in their velvet box, unused, and smiled with his actual beak. Sophisticated enough. More than. The rose, a little thirsty, still faced two desks.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
